source.title: Which Retain Set Matters for LLM Unlearning? A Case Study on Entity Unlearning

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how entity unlearning affects retain-set utility. It does not test whether attacks recover targeted knowledge after unlearning, or whether unlearning removes that knowledge rather than blocking access.
record.gate_note: The paraphrasing experiment paraphrases retain-set questions and compares their utility drop; it is not a rephrasing attack to recover targeted forgotten knowledge. The paper's gradient analysis measures gradient norms, not access to or recovery of forgotten knowledge. Results in Table 1 on Forget Efficacy do not establish near-chance targeted accuracy. Appendix Table 13 contains hyperparameter comparisons; values used to select hyperparameters are not recorded as result rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how entity unlearning (GA, NPO, IDK, DPO) degrades utility on different retain-set neighbor sets. It reports no recovery attack of any kind on forgotten knowledge: no relearning, ablation, quantization, or prompting. Its paraphrases are of retain-set questions, not forget-set questions. Forget Efficacy is a composite score that hyperparameter tuning holds at 0.65–0.75, not targeted accuracy measured against chance. Its results therefore bear on no version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that syntactic similarity, more than domain or entity ties, drives retained-knowledge degradation during entity unlearning. They also find that regularizing on syntactically similar neighbors best preserves utility, while matching or beating other sets elsewhere.
record.recipe_differences: Applies entity-unlearning methods GA, DPO, NPO, and IDK to study retain-set effects; it does not implement or test the recovery-attack recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Retain-set utility drop varies with neighbor-set type, syntactic similarity, entity category, and unlearning method. The paper reports a difference between syntactically similar and dissimilar retain-set questions even after paraphrasing.

fits_no_version.finding: After entity unlearning, retain questions syntactically similar to forget questions lose more utility than domain- or entity-neighbor questions (e.g., Table 6 GA: SynSimilar 0.770→0.375 vs Entity 0.712→0.411). The pattern persists under paraphrase (Table 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Entity unlearning causes collateral utility loss concentrated on retain questions that share syntactic form with the forget set.

fits_no_version.finding: In the syntactically similar set, non-human entity categories show larger utility drops than the Human category across most methods (Table 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Collateral utility loss from entity unlearning varies by entity category.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study is limited to entity unlearning and mid-sized models, as the authors note. It does not evaluate recovery attacks, and uncertainty estimates are not stated for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Tables 8–10 report many regularization train/test-set configurations; these are omitted because they concern retain-set regularization rather than recovery of targeted knowledge, and recording all combinations would exceed the row limit. Figure-only relative utility-drop and gradient-norm plots are also not separately rowed where the corresponding retain-set findings are represented by tables.

untested.parts: No targeted-accuracy-vs-chance measurement (only composite Forget Efficacy, tuned to 0.65–0.75). No general benchmark such as MMLU. No attack on the unlearned model.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation. No analysis of blocking versus deletion; the gradient-norm analysis concerns retain-set interference.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack on forget-set knowledge; paraphrasing is applied only to retain-set questions.
No method is claimed to be, or tested as, robust to recovery attacks; syntactic-neighbor regularization targets utility preservation only.

record.verdict_notes: Lynch et al. (Eight Methods) and WMDP are cited only as background. Forget-set rows are absent by design; Forget Efficacy is fixed by hyperparameter selection, so it is a selection value, not a result. Regularization Tables 8–10 concern utility preservation and are rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance, general ability alongside it, or simple attacks on an unlearned model.
No post-unlearning relearning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of whether the method blocks access rather than deletes knowledge.
No prompting-only attack to recover targeted forgotten knowledge. The paraphrasing experiment concerns retain-set questions.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the attacks in the claim.
